subtopic: 1.4.2 Data Structures (part 2 — trees, graphs, hash tables)
objectives: I can define a tree and a binary search tree, and build a BST from a given insertion order.
I can add nodes to and remove nodes from a BST so the ordering property still holds.
I can state the order in which depth-first (post-order) and breadth-first traversals visit nodes.
I can represent a graph as an adjacency matrix or adjacency list, and explain how a hash table achieves O(1) lookup and handles collisions.

retrieval.q: From week 19: when inserting node N between nodes A and B in a linked list, which pointer is written first?
retrieval.a: N's next pointer is set to B first, then A's next is set to N; the reverse order loses the route to the rest of the list.

retrieval.q: From week 19: a circular queue of size 6 has rear = 5. What does rear become after the next enqueue, and why?
retrieval.a: rear = (5 + 1) MOD 6 = 0; the MOD wrap reuses cells freed by earlier dequeues.

retrieval.q: From week 18: an empty stack receives push(2), push(6), pop(), push(9), pop(), pop(). List the values returned in order.
retrieval.a: 6, 9, 2 (LIFO: each pop returns the most recent unpopped push).

retrieval.q: From week 19: deleting the node holding 15 from the list 12 -> 15 -> 22 needs one pointer change. State it.
retrieval.a: 12's next pointer is set to the node holding 22; the 15 node becomes unreachable garbage.

retrieval.q: From week 18: give one structural difference between a record and an array.
retrieval.a: A record has named fields that may hold different types; an array has indexed elements all of one type.

keywords.def: A connected, hierarchical structure with no cycles: one root, then parents, children and leaves.
A binary tree where every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree larger values.
Visit the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node itself; the root comes last.
Visit nodes level by level from the root, left to right, using a queue of discovered nodes.
A set of vertices connected by edges; may be directed, undirected or weighted, and may contain cycles.
A 2D array where cell [i][j] records whether (or at what weight) an edge joins vertex i to vertex j.
A list, for each vertex, of its neighbours; stores only edges that exist, suiting sparse graphs.
Two different keys hashing to the same index; resolved by chaining or by rehashing to another slot.

content.heading: Trees: hierarchy without cycles
points: A tree is connected and acyclic: exactly one route exists between any two nodes.
Vocabulary: the root at the top, edges (branches) down to children, each child has one parent.
A leaf has no children; a node plus all its descendants forms a subtree.
Uses: file systems, organisation charts, HTML page structure, game move trees.

content.heading: Binary trees and the BST ordering rule
points: A binary tree allows each node at most two children: left and right.
A binary search tree adds an ordering rule: left subtree < node < right subtree.
The rule applies to whole subtrees, not just immediate children: every left descendant is smaller.
A BST is not just any binary tree: without the ordering property, fast searching is impossible.
Searching halves the remaining tree at each step: O(log n) comparisons when balanced.

content.heading: Building a BST: insertion order decides shape
points: To add a value, compare from the root: smaller goes left, larger goes right, repeat until an empty spot.
New values always join the tree as leaves; existing nodes never move.
The same values inserted in a different order produce a differently shaped tree.
Sorted input builds a one-sided chain: effectively a linked list, so search degrades to O(n).
content.note: Exam habit: always process the insertion list strictly left to right, drawing after every value.

content.heading: Removing nodes from a BST
points: Removing a leaf is trivial: the parent's pointer to it becomes null.
Removing a node with one child: the parent bypasses it, pointing at the child (like a linked list delete).
Removing a node with two children: replace its value with its in-order successor, the smallest value in its right subtree.
That successor has no left child, so deleting it from its old position is one of the easy cases.
After any removal the ordering rule must still hold everywhere: check by reading the tree left to right.

content.heading: Depth-first (post-order) traversal
points: Rule: visit the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node itself.
It plunges deep before going wide; a node is only visited once both its subtrees are finished.
The root is therefore always visited last.
Uses: safely deleting a whole tree (children before parents) and producing postfix expressions.
Under the hood it uses a stack: the recursion from 2.2.1 stacks each unfinished node.
content.note: Here you must give the visiting ORDER; writing the full recursive algorithm belongs to 2.3.1 later this year.

content.heading: Breadth-first traversal
points: Rule: visit nodes level by level from the root, left to right within each level.
It uses a queue: visit a node, enqueue its children, dequeue the next node to visit.
The root is visited first: the opposite end of the order from post-order.
Uses: finding the shallowest occurrence of something, and level-by-level processing.
Notice last fortnight's structures returning: depth-first rides a stack, breadth-first rides a queue.

content.heading: Graphs: vertices and edges
points: A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges; cycles are allowed and there is no root.
Undirected edges work both ways; directed edges (arrows) are one-way, like Twitter follows.
Weighted edges carry a cost: distance, time or price on each connection.
Uses: road maps, computer networks, social networks, the web's link structure.
A tree is really a special graph: connected, undirected and containing no cycles.

content.heading: Adjacency matrix vs adjacency list
points: Matrix: a V x V grid; cell [i][j] holds 1 (or the weight) if an edge joins i to j, else 0.
Undirected graphs give a symmetric matrix; edge lookup is a single cell read, O(1).
But the matrix always costs V squared cells, mostly zeros in a sparse graph.
List: each vertex stores just its neighbours (with weights if needed); memory grows with edges, not vertices squared.
Choose matrix for dense graphs or constant edge tests; list for large, sparse graphs like road maps.

content.heading: Hash tables: from key to index in one step
points: A hash function turns a key into an array index, for example index = key MOD tableSize.
The record is stored at that computed index: no searching happens at all.
Lookup recomputes the hash: the same key always gives the same index, so retrieval is direct, O(1).
Uses: username and password lookup, caches, compiler symbol tables, Python dictionaries.
Contrast: a hash table finds one key instantly but holds no ordering; a BST keeps order but costs O(log n).

content.heading: Collisions and how to handle them
points: A collision is two different keys hashing to the same index: inevitable, not a fault.
Chaining: each index holds a linked list; colliding items join the chain, searched linearly.
Rehashing (e.g. linear probing): apply a rule such as step to the next free cell, wrapping at the end.
Searching retraces exactly the same probes; reaching an empty cell proves the key is absent.
As the table fills (load factor rises), chains and probe runs grow, and lookup drifts away from O(1).

worked_examples.title: Building a BST from 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 — then removing 30
steps: 50 enters the empty tree as the root.
30 < 50, so 30 becomes the left child of 50. 70 > 50, so 70 becomes the right child.
20: less than 50 (go left), less than 30: left child of 30. 40: less than 50, greater than 30: right child of 30.
60: greater than 50 (go right), less than 70: left child of 70. 80: greater than 50, greater than 70: right child of 70.
Shape: root 50; 30 has children 20 and 40; 70 has children 60 and 80. Perfectly balanced, three levels.
Comprehension check: 65 would walk 50 (right), 70 (left), 60 (right): new right child of 60.
Remove 30, a node with two children: replace its value with its in-order successor, 40, the smallest value in its right subtree.
The old 40 node was a leaf, so it is simply detached. The left subtree now reads 20, 40 and the ordering rule still holds everywhere.

worked_examples.title: Traversing the original 50/30/70 tree both ways
steps: Depth-first (post-order) rule: left subtree, right subtree, then the node itself.
Left subtree of 50 (rooted at 30): its left leaf 20, its right leaf 40, then 30: giving 20, 40, 30.
Right subtree of 50 (rooted at 70): 60, then 80, then 70: giving 60, 80, 70.
The root comes last. Full post-order: 20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50.
Breadth-first uses a queue: visit 50, then level two left to right (30, 70), then level three (20, 40, 60, 80).
Full breadth-first: 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80. It matches the insertion order here only because this tree happens to be balanced: that is a coincidence, not a rule.
Contrast for later: in-order (left, node, right) would give 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80: ascending, straight from the BST property.

worked_examples.title: One graph, two representations: undirected edges A-B, A-C, B-C, C-D
steps: The graph has 4 vertices and 4 edges; D connects only to C.
Adjacency matrix (rows and columns A, B, C, D): row A: 0 1 1 0; row B: 1 0 1 0; row C: 1 1 0 1; row D: 0 0 1 0.
The matrix is symmetric because the graph is undirected, and it costs 4 x 4 = 16 cells however few edges exist.
Adjacency list: A: B, C. B: A, C. C: A, B, D. D: C. That is 8 entries, each edge recorded twice.
Edge test, is B joined to D? Matrix: read cell [B][D] instantly (0, no). List: scan B's neighbours A, C and conclude no.
Adding weights: each matrix cell holds the weight instead of 1; each list entry becomes a (neighbour, weight) pair.
Verdict: this small dense graph suits either; scale to a national road map (millions of vertices, few edges each) and the matrix's V squared zeros make the list the only sane choice.

activities.title: Grow-Your-Own BST
instructions: Seven students draw cards 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 and insert themselves in that order, the class chanting the rule each time: smaller goes left, larger goes right, walking from the root to an empty spot. Arms become branches.
Comprehension check: where would 65 go? Walk it: 50 right, 70 left, 60 right: new right child of 60.
Traversal walks: a volunteer walks depth-first (post-order: left, right, root) while the class records the sequence, then a second volunteer walks breadth-first level by level.
Rebuild the tree from sorted input 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80: a right-leaning chain appears, and the class counts search steps for 80 (7 versus 3 in the balanced tree).
Debrief: insertion order decides shape; balanced gives O(log n) search, a degenerate chain gives O(n).
activities.stretch: Remove the 30 student: the class must nominate the replacement (in-order successor 40) and justify why the ordering rule survives.

activities.title: Coat-Hook Hash Table
instructions: Seven chairs labelled 0 to 6 form the table; the hash function is index = key MOD 7, computed aloud by the class before each key-holder sits.

Insert 6 (sits at 6), then 15 (15 MOD 7 = 1). Insert 22: 22 MOD 7 = 1, chair taken: a collision. Agree linear probing (step right to the next empty chair, wrapping): 22 sits at 2. Insert 8: hashes to 1, probes past 1 and 2, sits at 3.
Search demo: find key 8. Hash to 1, compare chairs 1 (15), 2 (22), 3 (8): found in 3 comparisons.
Unsuccessful search: is 29 in the table? 29 MOD 7 = 1; probe chairs 1, 2, 3 (all wrong), chair 4 is empty: 29 is definitively absent.
Debrief: hashing gives near O(1) lookup; collisions are expected and handled; as chairs fill, probe chains grow and speed decays.
activities.stretch: Re-run resolving collisions by chaining (colliders queue behind chair 1) and compare the two searches for key 8.

activities.title: Which Structure Am I? Corners (full edition)
instructions: Corner signs: STACK, QUEUE, TREE/BST, HASH TABLE; the centre floor means something else, say what. Read a scenario; students walk; a delegate per corner justifies before the reveal.

Scenarios: (a) undo in a text editor; (b) print jobs for a shared printer; (c) 100,000 usernames needing near-instant login lookup; (d) a company organisation chart; (e) the browser back button; (f) keypresses buffered while the CPU is busy; (g) customer records listed alphabetically on demand; (h) a chessboard's 8 x 8 grid; (i) cities and the roads between them.

Answers: (a) stack; (b) queue; (c) hash table, O(1) lookup by key; (d) tree, one root, no cycles; (e) stack; (f) queue; (g) BST, ordered retrieval at O(log n); (h) centre: 2D array; (i) centre: graph, many-to-many with cycles, so not a tree.
After each reveal, ask the losing corners why their structure is worse here, not just why the winner is good.
activities.stretch: For scenario (i), ask whether an adjacency matrix or list suits a sparse national road map and why (list: memory grows with edges, not vertices squared).

practice.q: The values 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70 are inserted in that order into an empty binary search tree. Describe the resulting tree. [3]
practice.a: 40 is the root (1); 20 is its left child with children 10 and 30 (1); 60 is its right child with children 50 and 70, giving a balanced three-level tree (1).

practice.q: State the order a depth-first (post-order) traversal visits the nodes of that tree. [2]
practice.a: 10, 30, 20, 50, 70, 60, 40 (2 marks; 1 mark if the root 40 is correctly last but one subtree order slips).

practice.q: State the order a breadth-first traversal visits the same tree, and name the data structure the traversal relies on. [2]
practice.a: 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70 (1); it uses a queue of discovered nodes (1).

practice.q: Explain why inserting already-sorted data into a binary search tree harms search performance. [3]
practice.a: Each new value is larger than the last, so every insertion goes right (1); the tree degenerates into a one-sided chain, effectively a linked list (1); searching then takes O(n) comparisons instead of O(log n) (1).

practice.q: A social network has millions of users, each with relatively few friends. Justify representing it as an adjacency list rather than an adjacency matrix. [3]
practice.a: The graph is sparse (1); a matrix needs V squared cells, almost all zeros, which is wasteful at millions of vertices (1); a list stores only the edges that exist, so memory grows with friendships, not users squared (1).

practice.q: Describe how a hash table stores and retrieves a customer record using the account number as the key, and explain why lookup is fast. [4]
practice.a: A hash function is applied to the account number to compute an index (1); the record is stored at that index in the table (1); retrieval applies the same function to the same key, giving the same index (1); the record is accessed directly with no searching, so lookup is approximately O(1) (1).

practice.q: Keys 25, 13 and 34 are inserted into a hash table of size 7 using index = key MOD 7. State each index, identify the collision, and explain how chaining resolves it. [4]
practice.a: 25 MOD 7 = 4 (1); 13 MOD 7 = 6 (1); 34 MOD 7 = 6, colliding with 13 (1); with chaining, index 6 holds a linked list and 34 is appended behind 13, so both remain retrievable (1).

practice.q: A node with two children is removed from a binary search tree. Explain how the tree is restructured so the ordering property still holds. [3]
practice.a: The node's value is replaced by its in-order successor, the smallest value in its right subtree (or largest in its left) (1); that value is greater than everything in the left subtree and no larger than anything remaining in the right (1); the successor node is then deleted from its old position, which is a leaf or one-child case (1).

misconceptions: Students often think any binary tree is a binary search tree; a BST needs the ordering property, left subtree < node < right subtree, applied to whole subtrees.
Students often swap the traversal machinery: depth-first relies on a stack (or recursion), breadth-first on a queue, not the other way round.
Students often think insertion order into a BST does not matter; it fixes the shape, and sorted input collapses search from O(log n) to O(n).
Students often treat a collision as the hash function being broken or data being lost; collisions are expected and handled by chaining or rehashing.
Students often assume a hash table keeps data sorted; it does not, which is exactly why an ordered listing needs a BST instead.
exam_link: Command words seen here: draw or show for building a BST from an insertion order (2-4 marks), state for traversal orders (2 marks), justify or compare for matrix versus list (2-6 marks), describe for hash storage and lookup (3-4 marks).
At 1.4.2 the traversal question asks for the visiting order only; writing the recursive traversal algorithm is examined under 2.3.1.
Adjacency matrix versus adjacency list is a classic justify question: always quote the graph's density and the V squared memory cost.
Example stem: 'The following values are added to a binary search tree in the order given. Draw the tree, then state the order in which a post-order traversal visits the nodes.' [4]
task: Insert 45, 25, 65, 15, 35, 55, 75, 30 in that order into an empty BST and draw it. Write out the depth-first (post-order) and breadth-first traversal orders, then remove 25 and redraw the tree. (Shape: root 45; 25 has children 15 and 35, and 35 has left child 30; 65 has children 55 and 75. Post-order: 15, 30, 35, 25, 55, 75, 65, 45. Breadth-first: 45, 25, 65, 15, 35, 55, 75, 30. Removing 25: replace it with its in-order successor 30, which detaches from 35 as a leaf.)
challenge: A postcode lookup service must (a) return the address for a full postcode in near-constant time and (b) list all stored postcodes in alphabetical order on demand. Explain why no single structure from this topic does both jobs well, propose a combination of a hash table and a BST, and describe the cost of keeping both structures consistent every time a postcode is added or removed.

exit_ticket.q: In one sentence, what turns a binary tree into a binary search tree?
exit_ticket.a: Every node's left subtree holds only smaller values and its right subtree only larger values.

exit_ticket.q: Which traversal visits the root last, and which structure does breadth-first traversal rely on?
exit_ticket.a: Depth-first (post-order) visits the root last; breadth-first relies on a queue.

exit_ticket.q: Two keys hash to index 3. State the term for this and one way to resolve it.
exit_ticket.a: A collision; resolve by chaining (a linked list at that index) or by rehashing/probing to another free slot.
